    "Hermeneutical injustice 
    Hermeneutical injustice is injustice related to how people interpret their lives. (The word 'hermeneutical', which comes from the Greek word for 'interpreter', means 'pertaining to interpretation'.) 
    
    To understand this kind of injustice, it is useful to consider a concrete example. In the 1970s, the label "sexual harassment" was introduced to describe something that many people, especially women, had experienced since time immemorial.[2] Imagine the year is 1960, before the label was introduced. Consider a woman who experiences sexual harassment in this year. She may have difficulty putting her experience into words. The difficulty that she faces is no accident. It is due (in part) to women's exclusion from full participation in the shaping of the English language. Now imagine it is 1980. The woman may now better understand what has happened to her. However, she may struggle to explain this experience to someone else, because the concept of sexual harassment is not yet well known. The difficulty she faces is, again, no accident. It is due (in part) to women's exclusion from equal participation in the institutions and industries devoted to making sense of, describing, and explaining human experiences - such as journalism, publishing, and academia. Miranda Fricker argues that women's unequal participation in the shaping of the categories through which we all understand the world makes some women's lives less intelligible, whether to themselves or to others. What is true of women here is also true of other marginalized groups.
    
    Hermeneutical injustice occurs when someone's experiences are not well understood - by themselves or by others - because these experiences do not fit any concepts known to them (or known to others), due to the historic exclusion of some groups of people from activities, such as scholarship and journalism, that shape which concepts become well known.[3]"

rating.reasoning_summary: This strand traces the evolution of 'hermeneutical injustice' from academic concept to communal practice across 5 years (2020-2025). The boundary object is Miranda Fricker's Wikipedia screenshot explaining how marginalized groups lack vocabulary for their experiences. The arc moves from Covid-era 'sensemaking' critiques (March 2020) through Nosilverv's viral post (August 2020) reframing Twitter writing as hermeneutical labor, to Natural_hazard's mechanistic refinement (language acts via common knowledge, not individual cognition), culminating in 2025 memes about the futility of sense-making itself. title: “Make it make sense” broke, communal sensemaking woke
summary:
The most quotable shift was @natural_hazard’s dunk on the whole “words control thoughts” story: Newspeak/hermeneutical injustice doesn’t mainly stop you having thoughts — it isolates you from *common knowledge* that anyone else shares them. “Other people *are* our minds,” they say, and missing language hurts because it removes the social backing that makes an experience feel real/safe to name.

This whole mini-genre kicks off in early-Covid sensemaking discourse: @frideswyth side-eyes people begging for “sensemaking” like the pandemic is some brand-new revelation, and @m_ashcroft snaps that “give me sensemaking because I don’t want to have to develop agency.” Then August 2020 hits and @nosilverv drops the viral Wikipedia screenshot on Miranda Fricker’s “hermeneutical injustice” with the command: “Read this… and understand why your life doesn’t make immediate sense… you need ‘communal sense-making’.” @DRMacIver celebrates like a friend finally joined his niche fandom, and @nosilverv escalates it into a lifestyle prescription: write on Twitter, talk to friends/therapists — because “normies are just structurally hermeneutically privileged.” People riff (and nitpick): @myhandle counters that plenty of “normies” are anxious in therapy too; @dbabbitt turns it into a definitional gotcha (“is it hermeneutic injustice to demand you define ‘fascist’?”). The peak is when the concept stops being an academic term and becomes a justification for why online oversharing and endless threads feel *necessary*.

After that, the vibe curdles: @nosilverv starts yelling “Stop being crippled by your felt necessity to make sense!” and @natural_hazard lands the bleak practical corollary in 2022: “making sense only makes sense if others are willing to make sense of the sense you’re making” (with a whole subway-car example of being socially ignored accelerating “crazy” behavior). By 2024–2025 it’s basically memes and resignation: @visakanv says you can’t enjoy the site expecting coherence, @Malcolm_Ocean claims there’s “other sense on the far side of nonsense,” and @grantbels closes the loop with a poetic rejection of linear sensemaking as the main tool for living. Why care: it’s a pretty sharp explanation for why marginalized/isolated people end up doing “too much” public narration — they’re not just venting, they’re trying to manufacture the shared reality that makes their experience legible in the first place.
